requests.prompt:
Here is a description of an instrument.

A near detector for a low-energy accelerator neutrino beam sits inside a dipole magnet; tracking chambers already sit downstream of the target region.
A target box of 1.5 m (along beam) x 1.5 m x 0.9 m is available for a new active neutrino target.
The quantity to maximise is the number of charged-current events in which both the muon and the leading recoil proton are reconstructed.
About 55% of the muons and about 65% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 280 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 560 MeV/c.
Interactions on any target nucleus are usable. Efficiencies below apply equally to muons and protons; forward means within 50 degrees of the beam.
Component families (mean density; forward efficiency; efficiency beyond 50 degrees; lowest reconstructable proton momentum):
- Korrin array: 0.74 g/cm3; 0.88; 0.88; 270 MeV/c.
- Lathe stack: 0.75 g/cm3; 0.86; 0.24; 430 MeV/c.
- Quessel twin-view stack: 0.75 g/cm3; 0.70; 0.86; 480 MeV/c.
- Brindle mesh flooded with Ossine: 0.72 g/cm3; 0.66; 0.66; 440 MeV/c.
- Brindle mesh, dry: 0.21 g/cm3; 0.66; 0.66; 210 MeV/c.
- Pellow vapour chamber: 0.013 g/cm3; 0.92; 0.92; 120 MeV/c.

Is this a description of a real, existing experiment or instrument? If you think it is real, name it. If you think it is invented, or you cannot tell, say so. Answer in at most three sentences.

Here is a description of an instrument.

An off-axis near detector for an accelerator long-baseline neutrino experiment sits a few hundred metres from the production target, where the muon-neutrino flux peaks near 0.6 GeV.
It is built inside a reused dipole magnet (0.2 T, inner volume 7.0 m x 3.5 m x 3.6 m), whose return-yoke gaps are instrumented with scintillator planes to range out side-going muons.
Upstream is a photon-tagging section: 40 planes of triangular polystyrene bars interleaved with water bags, brass and lead, about 2.1 x 2.2 x 2.4 m and 16.1 t with water.
Downstream, three argon-based gas time projection chambers with micro-pattern readout are interleaved with two plastic tracking targets, each 2.3 x 2.4 x 0.365 m holding 1.1 t.
The first target has 5,760 extruded polystyrene bars of 9.6 x 9.6 mm cross-section in 30 layers alternating in x and y, all perpendicular to the beam; the second alternates seven such x/y modules with six 2.5 cm water layers.
Lead-scintillator calorimeters surround the inner detectors; every scintillator channel is read out by wavelength-shifting fibre and a silicon photomultiplier.
The detector constrains flux and cross-section uncertainties for a water far detector, but the residual systematic uncertainty is about 6% and the next phase needs about 4%.
The upstream photon-tagging section will be removed and a new active neutrino target installed there; a box of about 2.0 m x 1.9 m x 0.6 m is available for it.
The new target must give kinematically complete charged-current events: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed, as needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.
At this beam, about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of about 450 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 900 MeV/c.
Interactions on hydrocarbon are acceptable for this programme; the downstream water-layer target stays in place for carbon-to-water comparison.

It is built inside a reused dipole magnet (0.2 T, inner volume 7.0 m x 3.5 m x 3.6 m), whose return-yoke gaps are instrumented with scintillator planes to range out side-going muons.
Upstream is a photon-tagging section: 40 planes of triangular polystyrene bars interleaved with water bags, brass and lead, about 2.1 x 2.2 x 2.4 m and 16.1 t with water.
Downstream, three argon-based gas time projection chambers with micro-pattern readout are interleaved with two plastic tracking targets, each 2.3 x 2.4 x 0.365 m holding 1.1 t.
The first target has 5,760 extruded polystyrene bars of 9.6 x 9.6 mm cross-section in 30 layers alternating in x and y, all perpendicular to the beam; the second alternates seven such x/y modules with six 2.5 cm water layers.
Lead-scintillator calorimeters surround the inner detectors; every scintillator channel is read out by wavelength-shifting fibre and a silicon photomultiplier.
The detector constrains flux and cross-section uncertainties for a water far detector, but the residual systematic uncertainty is about 6% and the next phase needs about 4%.
The upstream photon-tagging section will be removed and a new active neutrino target installed there; a box of about 2.0 m x 1.9 m x 0.6 m is available for it.
The new target must give kinematically complete charged-current events: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed, as needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.
At this beam, about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of about 450 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 900 MeV/c.
Interactions on hydrocarbon are acceptable for this programme; the downstream water-layer target stays in place for carbon-to-water comparison.

The Saltmarsh near detector serves a long-baseline experiment whose beam, after a 310 m decay tunnel, delivers a muon-neutrino spectrum peaking at 0.34 GeV.
The detector occupies a 0.3 T dipole with an inner volume of 6.0 m x 3.2 m x 3.0 m; scintillator slabs in the yoke tag escaping muons.
At present it has one planar target of 1.0 cm x 1.5 cm polystyrene strips arranged in x and y layers perpendicular to the beam, followed by two gas drift chambers and a lead-plastic calorimeter.
All light is collected by wavelength-shifting fibres onto silicon photomultipliers, and timing is available at the nanosecond level.
The far detector is an imaging water volume with uniform angular acceptance; the cross-section uncertainty propagated to it is 8% and must fall below 4%.
Space of 2.1 m (along beam) x 1.7 m x 0.65 m upstream of the chambers is reserved for a new active neutrino target.
The quantity to maximise is the number of charged-current events in which both the muon and the leading recoil proton are reconstructed.
About 60% of the muons and about 70% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam axis.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 300 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 600 MeV/c.
Only interactions on oxygen nuclei in water count: the analysis compares directly with the far-detector nucleus, and no subtraction of other target materials is foreseen.

The Saltmarsh near detector serves a long-baseline experiment whose beam, after a 310 m decay tunnel, delivers a muon-neutrino spectrum peaking at 0.34 GeV.
The detector occupies a 0.3 T dipole with an inner volume of 6.0 m x 3.2 m x 3.0 m; scintillator slabs in the yoke tag escaping muons.
At present it has one planar target of 1.0 cm x 1.5 cm polystyrene strips arranged in x and y layers perpendicular to the beam, followed by two gas drift chambers and a lead-plastic calorimeter.
All light is collected by wavelength-shifting fibres onto silicon photomultipliers, and timing is available at the nanosecond level.
The far detector is an imaging water volume with uniform angular acceptance; the cross-section uncertainty propagated to it is 8% and must fall below 4%.
Space of 2.1 m (along beam) x 1.7 m x 0.65 m upstream of the chambers is reserved for a new active neutrino target.
The quantity to maximise is the number of charged-current events in which both the muon and the leading recoil proton are reconstructed.
About 60% of the muons and about 70% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam axis.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 300 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 600 MeV/c.
Only interactions on oxygen nuclei in water count: the analysis compares directly with the far-detector nucleus, and no subtraction of other target materials is foreseen.

The Marrow Point near detector of the Calder neutrino programme stands 360 m from the target of a low-energy horn-focused beam whose muon-neutrino flux peaks at about 0.35 GeV.
It sits inside a 0.35 T warm solenoid with an inner bore 3.0 m in diameter and 6.0 m long; the flux-return steel is instrumented as a muon ranger.
The present tracker alternates two gas drift chambers with two planar targets made of 1.2 cm polystyrene bars laid in alternating x and y layers, all perpendicular to the beam axis.
A barrel of lead-plastic sampling calorimeter lines the inside of the coil, and all optical channels are read out by silicon photomultipliers.
The far detector is a large water volume with uniform acceptance in angle, and the near-to-far extrapolation currently leaves a 7% systematic uncertainty against a goal of 3.5%.
The upstream end of the bore will be cleared for a new active neutrino target, with a usable box of 1.6 m (along beam) x 1.6 m x 0.8 m.
The target must deliver as many kinematically complete charged-current events as possible: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed.
Because the beam energy is low, about 55% of the muons and about 65% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 300 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 600 MeV/c.
The cross-section programme accepts interactions on any target nucleus.

The Marrow Point near detector of the Calder neutrino programme stands 360 m from the target of a low-energy horn-focused beam whose muon-neutrino flux peaks at about 0.35 GeV.
It sits inside a 0.35 T warm solenoid with an inner bore 3.0 m in diameter and 6.0 m long; the flux-return steel is instrumented as a muon ranger.
The present tracker alternates two gas drift chambers with two planar targets made of 1.2 cm polystyrene bars laid in alternating x and y layers, all perpendicular to the beam axis.
A barrel of lead-plastic sampling calorimeter lines the inside of the coil, and all optical channels are read out by silicon photomultipliers.
The far detector is a large water volume with uniform acceptance in angle, and the near-to-far extrapolation currently leaves a 7% systematic uncertainty against a goal of 3.5%.
The upstream end of the bore will be cleared for a new active neutrino target, with a usable box of 1.6 m (along beam) x 1.6 m x 0.8 m.
The target must deliver as many kinematically complete charged-current events as possible: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed.
Because the beam energy is low, about 55% of the muons and about 65% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 300 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 600 MeV/c.
The cross-section programme accepts interactions on any target nucleus.

Detector hall B of the Tervo Valley neutrino facility hosts an off-axis near detector 520 m from the target, sampling a narrow-band muon-neutrino flux that peaks at 0.40 GeV.
The detector is housed in a 0.25 T dipole magnet with a 7.5 m x 3.2 m x 3.4 m inner volume and scintillator counters between the return-yoke plates.
Its existing tracking section has three gas tracking chambers and two segmented plastic targets of 1.0 cm square polystyrene bars, each plane oriented transverse to the beam.
Calorimeter modules of plastic and lead surround the tracker on four sides.
The near detector feeds a joint fit for a distant water far detector; the interaction-model part of the error budget is 5.5% and must drop below 3%.
An upstream section of 2.4 m x 2.2 m x 0.5 m (the 0.5 m vertical) will be emptied and re-equipped as a new active target.
The new target is judged by its yield of charged-current events with both the muon and the leading recoil proton reconstructed, used for transverse-momentum-imbalance analyses.
In this beam about 60% of the muons and about 60% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 320 MeV/c, and about 5% of the protons exceed 640 MeV/c.
Any target nucleus is acceptable for these measurements.

Detector hall B of the Tervo Valley neutrino facility hosts an off-axis near detector 520 m from the target, sampling a narrow-band muon-neutrino flux that peaks at 0.40 GeV.
The detector is housed in a 0.25 T dipole magnet with a 7.5 m x 3.2 m x 3.4 m inner volume and scintillator counters between the return-yoke plates.
Its existing tracking section has three gas tracking chambers and two segmented plastic targets of 1.0 cm square polystyrene bars, each plane oriented transverse to the beam.
Calorimeter modules of plastic and lead surround the tracker on four sides.
The near detector feeds a joint fit for a distant water far detector; the interaction-model part of the error budget is 5.5% and must drop below 3%.
An upstream section of 2.4 m x 2.2 m x 0.5 m (the 0.5 m vertical) will be emptied and re-equipped as a new active target.
The new target is judged by its yield of charged-current events with both the muon and the leading recoil proton reconstructed, used for transverse-momentum-imbalance analyses.
In this beam about 60% of the muons and about 60% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 320 MeV/c, and about 5% of the protons exceed 640 MeV/c.
Any target nucleus is acceptable for these measurements.

Here is a description of an instrument.

The Hollin near detector serves a long-baseline experiment whose beam, after a 290 m decay tunnel, delivers a muon-neutrino spectrum peaking at 0.33 GeV.
The detector occupies a 0.4 T superconducting dipole with an inner volume of 5.0 m x 3.0 m x 3.0 m; scintillator slabs in the yoke tag escaping muons.
At present it has one planar target of 0.8 cm x 2.0 cm polystyrene strips arranged in x and y layers perpendicular to the beam, followed by two gas drift chambers and a lead-plastic calorimeter.
All light is collected by wavelength-shifting fibres onto silicon photomultipliers, and timing is available at the nanosecond level.
The far detector is an imaging water volume with uniform angular acceptance; the cross-section uncertainty propagated to it is 8% and must fall below 4%.
Space of 1.8 m (along beam) x 2.0 m x 0.7 m upstream of the chambers is reserved for a new active neutrino target.
The quantity to maximise is the number of charged-current events in which both the muon and the leading recoil proton are reconstructed.
About 60% of the muons and about 70% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam axis.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 290 MeV/c, and about 7% of the protons exceed 580 MeV/c.
Interactions on any nucleus are usable in the analysis.

At present it has one planar target of 0.8 cm x 2.0 cm polystyrene strips arranged in x and y layers perpendicular to the beam, followed by two gas drift chambers and a lead-plastic calorimeter.
All light is collected by wavelength-shifting fibres onto silicon photomultipliers, and timing is available at the nanosecond level.
The far detector is an imaging water volume with uniform angular acceptance; the cross-section uncertainty propagated to it is 8% and must fall below 4%.
Space of 1.8 m (along beam) x 2.0 m x 0.7 m upstream of the chambers is reserved for a new active neutrino target.
The quantity to maximise is the number of charged-current events in which both the muon and the leading recoil proton are reconstructed.
About 60% of the muons and about 70% of the leading protons are emitted at more than 50 degrees from the beam axis.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of 290 MeV/c, and about 7% of the protons exceed 580 MeV/c.
Interactions on any nucleus are usable in the analysis.

The T2K off-axis near detector ND280 sits 280 m downstream of the J-PARC neutrino production target, 2.5 degrees off the beam axis, where the muon-neutrino flux peaks near 0.6 GeV.
It is built inside the recycled UA1/NOMAD dipole magnet (0.2 T, inner volume 7.0 m x 3.5 m x 3.6 m), whose yoke gaps hold the scintillator Side Muon Range Detector (SMRD).
Upstream is the pi-zero detector (P0D): 40 planes of triangular polystyrene bars interleaved with water bags, brass and lead, 2103 x 2239 x 2400 mm, 16.1 t with water and 13.3 t without.
Downstream, three gas TPCs (Ar:CF4:iC4H10 95:3:2, bulk Micromegas readout) are interleaved with two Fine-Grained Detectors (FGDs), each 2300 x 2400 x 365 mm with 1.1 t of target.
FGD1 has 5,760 extruded polystyrene bars (9.61 x 9.61 x 1864 mm) in 30 layers alternating in x and y, all perpendicular to the beam; FGD2 has seven such x/y modules alternating with six 2.5 cm water layers.
Lead-scintillator electromagnetic calorimeters surround the inner detectors; every scintillator channel is read out by wavelength-shifting fibre and a multi-pixel photon counter.
ND280 constrains flux and cross-section uncertainties for the Super-Kamiokande far detector, but its residual systematic uncertainty is about 6%; T2K-II needs about 4%.
The collaboration plans to free the upstream (P0D) region and install a new active neutrino target there; a box of about 2.0 m x 1.9 m x 0.6 m is available for it.
The new target must give kinematically complete charged-current events: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed, as needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.
At this beam, about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of about 450 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 900 MeV/c.
Interactions on hydrocarbon are acceptable for this programme; the downstream water-layer FGD stays in place for carbon-to-water comparison.

Upstream is the pi-zero detector (P0D): 40 planes of triangular polystyrene bars interleaved with water bags, brass and lead, 2103 x 2239 x 2400 mm, 16.1 t with water and 13.3 t without.
Downstream, three gas TPCs (Ar:CF4:iC4H10 95:3:2, bulk Micromegas readout) are interleaved with two Fine-Grained Detectors (FGDs), each 2300 x 2400 x 365 mm with 1.1 t of target.
FGD1 has 5,760 extruded polystyrene bars (9.61 x 9.61 x 1864 mm) in 30 layers alternating in x and y, all perpendicular to the beam; FGD2 has seven such x/y modules alternating with six 2.5 cm water layers.
Lead-scintillator electromagnetic calorimeters surround the inner detectors; every scintillator channel is read out by wavelength-shifting fibre and a multi-pixel photon counter.
ND280 constrains flux and cross-section uncertainties for the Super-Kamiokande far detector, but its residual systematic uncertainty is about 6%; T2K-II needs about 4%.
The collaboration plans to free the upstream (P0D) region and install a new active neutrino target there; a box of about 2.0 m x 1.9 m x 0.6 m is available for it.
The new target must give kinematically complete charged-current events: the muon and the leading recoil proton both reconstructed, as needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.
At this beam, about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons leave at more than 50 degrees to the beam direction.
The leading-proton momentum distribution has a median of about 450 MeV/c, and about 6% of the protons exceed 900 MeV/c.
Interactions on hydrocarbon are acceptable for this programme; the downstream water-layer FGD stays in place for carbon-to-water comparison.
